title: Thomas More and Erasmus
hookLine: two friends, a book called Utopia, and humor with holiness

cards: A scholar is riding on horseback, the long way back from Italy to England, with hours to fill.
Rather than waste them, he starts composing a joke in his head: a whole book spoken by Folly herself, a lady who praises fools and mocks the wise.
He's on his way to stay with a friend in London, and the friend's name gives him the title. The scholar is Erasmus. The friend is Thomas More.

teach.b: Start with the pun. Erasmus wrote the book in Latin with a Greek title, Moriae Encomium, the Praise of Folly. In his letter to More at the front, he explains: moria is Greek for folly, and it sounds like More's name.
His friend, he adds, is as far from folly as his name is close to it. A joke between friends, printed in a book.

teach.h: A FACE THAT LEANS TOWARD CHEER.
teach.b: Erasmus once wrote a long letter describing More for someone who had never met him: a face that leans toward cheerfulness, a love of jokes from boyhood, a knack for finding something to enjoy in almost anyone, and at the same time a man serious about prayer and generous to the poor.
Then, More's own book, Utopia. A traveler describes an island run differently: property shared, gold despised, worship tolerant. The name is a made-up word, and the book plays games with it.
Readers still argue about how much More meant and how much was a joke with a sting in it. That uncertainty is part of the fun. Finally, holiness.
More is a canonized saint, and the stories told about his last days say he kept joking to the end. Wit, for him, didn't compete with faith.
In the Douay-Rheims, Ecclesiastes says there is "A time to weep, and a time to laugh." These two friends seem to have taken both halves of that line seriously.

how: Catholics honor Saint Thomas More, with Saint John Fisher, on a shared feast in June; he is the patron of statesmen and politicians, and some lawyers' guilds take his name.

games.q: you're Erasmus, riding back from Italy to stay with your friend More. the ride is long. what do you do?
o: compose a book in your head, spoken by Folly.
games.why: he began the Praise of Folly, and named it with a pun on his friend's name.

practice: Bring to mind one friend you've laughed with until you couldn't stop: where you were, what set it off, their face. Let a smile come if it wants to.
If you pray, give thanks for that friend by name; if you don't, just stay with the memory and let it warm the room.

wordCard.voice: Utopia. Thomas More's book about an island run differently, written while trading jokes in Latin with his friend Erasmus. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: witty and holy. Laughter and prayer can share the same life. Until tomorrow.
